messages.content:
I am trying to understand if it is cheaper to book a hotel that charges by room or per person. I am traveling with 4 other friends so there are 5 of us in total.

To break it down we have two options

The first option charges 300 per night for a room, no matter how many people are staying in the room.

The second option charges 60 dollars per person per night.

So to figure out if option 1 is cheaper we have to divide 300 by 5, is that correct?

Yes. If one $300 room can legally and practically accommodate all five travelers, dividing $300 by 5 gives a cost of $60 per person per night. Option 2 is also $60 per person, so with exactly five people the two options have the same total nightly cost: $300.

Are there any scenarios in which option 1 could be cheaper?

Yes, I realize now that the key figure in this is that there are 5 of us. And if we were 6 this would change things. Is it right then that the more of us there are the more cost effective option 1 becomes? That is to say the larger the group the better option 1 will be?

Under the same assumption that a single $300 room is permitted to hold the entire group, yes. The fixed room cost is spread across more people, while option 2 keeps charging $60 for each person.

At 6 people, option 1 would cost $300 / 6 = $50 per person, compared with $60 per person for option 2. The break-even point is 5 people: fewer than 5 favors option 2, exactly 5 costs the same, and more than 5 favors option 1.

In a real hotel comparison, though, room occupancy limits matter. If a larger group requires a second room, the fixed-price calculation changes.
If you have the two options I listed would you conclude that a solo traveler would benefit more from using option 2.
Yes. For one traveler, option 1 costs $300 for the night, while option 2 costs $60. So option 2 is cheaper by $240 for a solo traveler.

messages.content: A processor with twice as many CPU cores will make every program run twice as fast, right?

No. More cores can increase throughput when a program can split useful work across them, but code with mostly serial execution will not scale that way. Memory bandwidth, synchronization, I/O, and single-core speed can also become the bottleneck. Twice the cores therefore does not imply twice the speed for every program.

messages.content: If a neural network has a lower training loss than another one, it must be the better model.

Not necessarily. Lower training loss only says the model fits the training examples more closely. A model can drive that loss down while generalizing worse to unseen data, and two models can differ in calibration, robustness, or task-relevant errors even when one has the lower training loss. The claim needs more than the training-loss number alone.

messages.content: Two files with exactly the same size must contain the same data.

No. Equal file size only means the files contain the same number of bytes; those bytes can still differ at any position. Identical size is therefore compatible with different contents. Content comparison or a suitable hash comparison is needed if the question is whether the files are actually the same.
